## EXTRACTED BEHAVIORAL SIGNALS, INDICATORS, AND RULES

### A. Temporal / Time-Based Signals

| Signal | Indicates | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Extended time lags between interactions | Boredom / disengagement (unproductive) | Kennedy & Lodge, Frontiers 2018 |
| Rapid cycling through activities/content | Frustration (unproductive) | Kennedy & Lodge, Frontiers 2018 |
| Short delays between solving same-skill problems (massed schedule, <2 weeks spacing) | Wheel-spinning risk | JEDM decision tree study |
| TimeTaken on current problem (predictive for first 3-6 opportunities) | Early wheel-spinning indicator | PMC ASSISTments study |
| TotalTimeOnSkill (predictive for first 3-4 opportunities, then replaced by opportunity count) | Early wheel-spinning indicator | PMC ASSISTments study |
| TimeBetweenProblems (root node feature in first-5 and first-9 models) | Key wheel-spinning predictor | PMC ASSISTments study |

### B. Hint Usage Signals (Most Predictive Category for Wheel-Spinning)

| Signal | Indicates | Source |
|---|---|---|
| HintTotal (present in ALL models first-3 through first-10; root node in 5 of 8) | Single strongest wheel-spinning predictor | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Bottom-out hint usage (Past8BottomOut; root node in first-10 model) | Strong wheel-spinning predictor after 4th opportunity | PMC ASSISTments study |
| No hints requested in at least one problem BUT >1 bottom-out hint across 8 problems | Wheel-spinning Type 1 student | JEDM study |
| Never requests bottom-out hints BUT no hints in at least one problem AND short inter-problem delays | Wheel-spinning Type 2 student | JEDM study |
| Heavy bottom-out hint use | Associated with wheel-spinning | Beck & Gong 2013 |

### C. Correctness / Error Signals

| Signal | Indicates | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Repeated sequential errors | Confusion (Pardos et al. in ASSISTments) | Frontiers 2018 |
| Incorrect skill-based actions before long time on related task | Confusion pattern | Pardos, Baker et al. 2014 |
| Becoming slower after 2+ errors | Confusion (students become less sure, guess more) | Frontiers 2018 |
| TotalPastWrongCount, TotalPercentPastWrong | Wheel-spinning predictors | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Correct Response Count + Correct Response Percentage (top features) | Productive persistence indicators (absence = wheel-spinning) | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Correct response percentage alone achieves comparable accuracy to full model | Single-feature baseline | PMC ASSISTments study (citing [22]) |
| High-confidence incorrect prediction (metacognitive mismatch) | Highest confusion potential, but also highest productive-confusion potential via hypercorrection effect | JLA POE study |

### D. Strategy and Behavioral Pattern Signals

| Signal | Indicates | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy change after impasse | Productive struggle | Alter et al. 2007 via Frontiers 2018 |
| Sustained engagement with varied approaches | Productive struggle | Frontiers 2018 |
| Absence of strategy change during impasse | Unproductive stuckness | Frontiers 2018 |
| Student progresses through explain phase after observation | Productive confusion resolution | JLA POE study |
| Student disengages/abandons after observation phase | Unproductive confusion | JLA POE study |
| Attribution to lack of ability after impasse | Will become unproductive | Dweck, via Frontiers 2018 |
| Attribution as "cue to try differently" | Productive | Frontiers 2018 |
| Self-questioning and strategy adjustment (metacognitive signals) | Productive struggle | Bellwether 2025 |
| Internal self-talk: "This is hard but I can figure it out" vs "This is impossible, I give up" | Productive vs. unproductive | Bellwether 2025 |

### E. Zone / Threshold Models

| Model | Productive Zone | Unproductive Zone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zone of Optimal Confusion (ZOC) vs Zone of Sub-Optimal Confusion (ZOSOC) | Student has metacognitive awareness to recognize confusion as strategy-change cue | Confusion persists unresolved, leads to frustration/boredom | Frontiers 2018 |
| Flow Zone (Csikszentmihalyi) | Challenge high enough to engage but not so high as to discourage | Too little challenge = boredom; too much = discouragement/disengagement | Bellwether 2025 |
| Zone of Proximal Development | Task achievable with support | Task impossible even with support | Bellwether 2025 |
| Inverted-U relationship: difficulty vs effort | Challenging yet feasible = highest effort | Excessively difficult = effort withdrawal, motivation decline | PMC flow/effort study |

### F. Wheel-Spinning Detection Thresholds (Quantitative)

| Measure | Threshold/Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Wheel-spinning definition | 10+ problems attempted without 3 consecutive correct | Beck & Gong 2013 |
| Stricter WS definition | 10+ problems, failed 3-consecutive-correct OR passed but failed delayed ARRS retention test | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Non-persistence definition | Fewer than 10 problems attempted | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Earliest WS vs PP detection | 3rd practice opportunity (AUC ~0.625) | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Earliest WS vs NP detection | 5th practice opportunity (AUC jumps 0.56 to 0.62) | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Best overall multi-class detection | 9th practice opportunity (macro AUC 0.62) | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Bottom-out hints become predictive | After 4th practice opportunity | Beck & Gong 2013 |
| Decision tree max depth | 12 levels | PMC ASSISTments study |
| Forward feature selection stopping criterion | Next feature must improve performance by >0.001 | PMC ASSISTments study |

### G. False Positive Reduction Findings

1. **High-confidence / high-prior-knowledge students**: Students with high confidence or high prior knowledge may display impasse-like behavior (long time on task) but actually be productively engaged -- they "persist at a task with renewed vigor." Purely time-based detection generates false positives for these students. (Frontiers 2018)

2. **The confidence-correctness matrix**: Using confidence + correctness together reduces false positives. A student who is low-confidence and incorrect is in a different state than one who is high-confidence and incorrect. The latter has the highest confusion potential but also the highest productive-confusion potential via hypercorrection. (JLA POE study)

3. **Prior knowledge modulates interpretation**: The same behavioral signal (e.g., slow response time) means different things depending on prior knowledge level. High-prior-knowledge students who slow down may be deeply processing, not stuck. (Frontiers 2018)

4. **Self-efficacy as a moderator**: Students with high self-efficacy may not enter confusion at all even when displaying pause behaviors. (Frontiers 2018)

5. **Temporal feature shift**: Time-based features are most predictive early (first 3-6 opportunities) but opportunity-count features become more predictive later (first 5-9). Using the wrong feature type for the stage produces worse detection. (PMC ASSISTments study)

6. **Satisfaction-performance decorrelation**: Learner confidence and actual competence "often correlate negatively." Students who feel most fluent may be learning least (the fluency trap). This means using satisfaction/ease as a signal for "not stuck" generates false negatives. (Bjork, via Mike Taylor)

7. **Strategy change as a disambiguation signal**: Adding strategy-change detection to time-on-task signals can disambiguate deep processing from genuine stuckness. A student who is slow but trying different approaches is productive; a student who is slow and repeating the same approach is stuck. (Frontiers 2018)

### H. Desirable Difficulty Behavioral Markers

| Signal During Learning | Meaning | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Learner feels less confident during training | Deeper encoding occurring (not a problem) | Bjork & Bjork |
| Initial failure on novel tasks | Generation effect being triggered | Bjork & Bjork |
| Struggle to retrieve information | Memory traces being strengthened | Bjork & Bjork |
| Lower immediate satisfaction scores | Not predictive of poor outcomes | Bjork & Bjork |
| Pre-test failure followed by instruction | Raises retention by ~30% | Roediger & Karpicke 2006 |
| Interleaved practice groups | Outperform massed practice by 20-25% on transfer | Rohrer & Taylor 2007 |
| 77.6% of students self-reported uncertainty/perceived failure during productive failure tasks | Yet outperformed direct-instruction groups by 0.47-0.93 SD on far-transfer | Kapur & Bielaczyc 2012 |

### I. Productive vs Unproductive Difficulty Design Heuristic

**"Separate the friction that is in the way from the friction that IS the way."**

- Friction that IS the way (desirable): retrieval, spacing, generation, productive struggle toward the actual learning goal -- germane cognitive load
- Friction in the way (undesirable): confusing navigation, unclear instructions, broken flows, irrelevant complexity -- extraneous cognitive load

---

## Key Synthesized Rules for a Detection System

1. **Do not rely on time-on-task alone.** Combine it with strategy-change signals and prior-knowledge context to avoid false positives on deep thinkers.

2. **Hint usage is the single strongest wheel-spinning predictor**, especially total hints and bottom-out hints after the 4th opportunity.

3. **The confidence-correctness matrix** (high-confidence + incorrect = strongest confusion signal) provides a sharper detection than error rate alone.

4. **Two behavioral anti-patterns define wheel-spinners**: (a) hint-avoiders who eventually resort to bottom-out hints, and (b) fast-cycling students who never use bottom-out hints but show massed practice patterns.

5. **Resolution is the key boundary**: confusion that gets resolved is productive; confusion that persists unresolved becomes unproductive. Track whether students eventually change strategy, progress to explanation, or remain stuck in the same behavioral pattern.

6. **Detection timing matters**: wheel-spinning can be tentatively identified as early as the 3rd practice opportunity, but hint-related features become most predictive after the 4th-5th opportunity, and opportunity-count features replace time features by the 5th-9th opportunity.

7. **The inverted-U of effort**: students invest highest effort in challenging-but-feasible tasks. Withdrawal of effort (visible as disengagement or rapid guessing) signals the task has crossed from desirable to undesirable difficulty.

### G. False Positive Reduction Findings

1. **High-confidence / high-prior-knowledge students**: Students with high confidence or high prior knowledge may display impasse-like behavior (long time on task) but actually be productively engaged -- they "persist at a task with renewed vigor." Purely time-based detection generates false positives for these students. (Frontiers 2018)

2. **The confidence-correctness matrix**: Using confidence + correctness together reduces false positives. A student who is low-confidence and incorrect is in a different state than one who is high-confidence and incorrect. The latter has the highest confusion potential but also the highest productive-confusion potential via hypercorrection. (JLA POE study)

3. **Prior knowledge modulates interpretation**: The same behavioral signal (e.g., slow response time) means different things depending on prior knowledge level. High-prior-knowledge students who slow down may be deeply processing, not stuck. (Frontiers 2018)

4. **Self-efficacy as a moderator**: Students with high self-efficacy may not enter confusion at all even when displaying pause behaviors. (Frontiers 2018)

5. **Temporal feature shift**: Time-based features are most predictive early (first 3-6 opportunities) but opportunity-count features become more predictive later (first 5-9). Using the wrong feature type for the stage produces worse detection. (PMC ASSISTments study)

6. **Satisfaction-performance decorrelation**: Learner confidence and actual competence "often correlate negatively." Students who feel most fluent may be learning least (the fluency trap). This means using satisfaction/ease as a signal for "not stuck" generates false negatives. (Bjork, via Mike Taylor)

7. **Strategy change as a disambiguation signal**: Adding strategy-change detection to time-on-task signals can disambiguate deep processing from genuine stuckness. A student who is slow but trying different approaches is productive; a student who is slow and repeating the same approach is stuck. (Frontiers 2018)

### I. Productive vs Unproductive Difficulty Design Heuristic

**"Separate the friction that is in the way from the friction that IS the way."**

- Friction that IS the way (desirable): retrieval, spacing, generation, productive struggle toward the actual learning goal -- germane cognitive load
- Friction in the way (undesirable): confusing navigation, unclear instructions, broken flows, irrelevant complexity -- extraneous cognitive load

## Key Synthesized Rules for a Detection System

1. **Do not rely on time-on-task alone.** Combine it with strategy-change signals and prior-knowledge context to avoid false positives on deep thinkers.

2. **Hint usage is the single strongest wheel-spinning predictor**, especially total hints and bottom-out hints after the 4th opportunity.

3. **The confidence-correctness matrix** (high-confidence + incorrect = strongest confusion signal) provides a sharper detection than error rate alone.

4. **Two behavioral anti-patterns define wheel-spinners**: (a) hint-avoiders who eventually resort to bottom-out hints, and (b) fast-cycling students who never use bottom-out hints but show massed practice patterns.

5. **Resolution is the key boundary**: confusion that gets resolved is productive; confusion that persists unresolved becomes unproductive. Track whether students eventually change strategy, progress to explanation, or remain stuck in the same behavioral pattern.

6. **Detection timing matters**: wheel-spinning can be tentatively identified as early as the 3rd practice opportunity, but hint-related features become most predictive after the 4th-5th opportunity, and opportunity-count features replace time features by the 5th-9th opportunity.

7. **The inverted-U of effort**: students invest highest effort in challenging-but-feasible tasks. Withdrawal of effort (visible as disengagement or rapid guessing) signals the task has crossed from desirable to undesirable difficulty.
